The EU was nearer balance in the early 2010s; by the late 2010s the US cover share of EU PDMP plasma had climbed into the mid-to-high thirties. The deficit area chart in the dashboard tracks that climb: liters short rise even when domestic collection programs expand, because demand outruns VNRD growth.

Also distinguish **source plasma** from **recovered plasma**, and **plasma for transfusion** from **plasma for fractionation**. Mixing those series invents fake self-sufficiency. This post tracks the fractionation feedstock that becomes PDMP.

South Asia** still follows near **8.5%**. US???EAP, US???South Asia, Europe???Africa/MENA, and Russia???Central Asia complete the ladder.

Open **Off-balance leverage**. Our [bank loan charge-offs](/blog/bank-loan-chargeoffs-2026) post tracks the loss tape; this lens tracks *who owns the dollars inside that tape*. A system can look ???fine??? on aggregate net charge-offs while cards still dominate the loss share and CRE still dominates the unresolved delinquency share.

The OECD donor bars beside them stay the milder tip: Germany ~**18%**, Japan **16%**, France **12%**, Top-3 **46%** of **$34.7B**. The instrument donut still shows **67%** loans / **29%** grants. So the Q3 story is not ???finance democratised.??? It is ???the largest institutional engine got larger (+**31%** YoY) while remaining bank-concentrated, and the bilateral tip remained plural-but-thin under a loan-heavy instrument mix.??? The [August update](/blog/adaptation-economics-update-202608) tracks the level bounce; this lens tracks *who inside the club* holds the tip.

The FRLD row is the extreme thin tip: even if Top-3 pledgers concentrate ~**61%** of a sub-billion pledge book, delivery remains ~**$449M** against multi-hundred-billion needs. Loss-and-damage capitalization is a political milestone and a rounding error on the residual ladder. Our [US billion-dollar weather disasters](/blog/us-billion-dollar-weather-disasters-2026) piece tracks the rich-country insured tape; this lens shows why that tape plus a sub-billion FRLD window still leaves households as Top-1.
- **GS IR** is a hyperscaler research path that can sit above or beside GI depending on year and bull/base ??? another reminder that ???AI capex??? is a family of stacks, not one ticker.
- **Do not splice China NBS yuan GERD (??3.93T domestic in 2025)** into PPP world shares; the [August 202608 update](/blog/measurement-science-update-202608) tracks that flow separately.

The share ?? tightness scatter on that view still puts CoWoS, EUV, leading-edge foundry, and AI GPUs in the upper-right cluster. Bubble size tracks HHI. Tightness and share remain related but not identical: HBM???s tightness stays **9** with ???only??? **55%** top-1 because the *set* is three vendors, not one.
"Dark navy cinematic data-viz of amber Top-1/Top-3 concentration bars beside glowing GPU racks and cyan high-voltage grid arcs",

The dual-ledger line keeps IEA central (~**950 TWh** in 2030) and Gartner (>**1,200 TWh**) on separate tracks. Do not average them. The gap (~**250 TWh**) is a forecast-dispersion meter. It does not move Top-1 / Top-3 shares by itself ??? but it does raise the stakes of *where* the next gigawatts land if the higher path proves closer to right.

Local intensity lollipops are unchanged for a reason. Virginia ~**25%** of state electricity and Ireland ~**20%** of metered supply are still an order of magnitude above the ~**1.5%** world average. Six US states remain above the **10%** threshold. Emerging and developing economies outside China still hold roughly **half** of internet users and **under 10%** of global data-centre capacity. The third hinge: **Q3 did not democratise siting.** Faster world TWh growth without geographic diversification simply packs more megawatts into the same political grids.

matches.content: 2024 was a year of market-size stability and sub-50 percent loss ratio performance for the U.S Cyber market. U.S. Cyber written premium reported to the NAIC decreased 2 percent year-over-year to $7.1 billion in 2024. At the same time, the U.S. industry loss ratio reported to the NAIC increased by 7 points to 49 percent in 2024, driven by increased frequency and decreased earned premium per policy.

Reflecting on last year???s report, calendar year 2023 data ??? which mostly covered business written in 2022 and 2023 ??? showed improved performance despite stalled premium growth in the U.S. Cyber market. This report cautioned of potential headwinds that could impact 2024 performance such as the CrowdStrike event and rebounding frequency.

In 2024, the market felt the effects of these headwinds which may have contributed to the loss ratio deterioration outlined in this report. Widespread events such as CrowdStrike, Change Healthcare and CDK struck the market, highlighting the potential materiality of catastrophe events and the importance of reinsurance. Furthermore, ransomware frequency continues to rise amongst a softening rate environment. Despite these challenges, the U.S. industry loss ratio allows for 51 points of margin for other expenses to remain profitable, demonstrating the resilience of the U.S. Cyber market.

In 2024, the total number of Cyber insurers reporting Cyber business to the NAIC remained the same and written premium per policy decreased. These factors contributed to a year-over-year written premium decrease from $7.25 billion to $7.08 billion.
Exhibit 1: U.S. Cyber direct written premiums | 2020 ??? 2024

The rate environment in the Cyber market is showing signs of improvement after a period of softening. Average written premium per policy fell by 1 percent from 2023 to 2024, which is a smaller change compared to 2023. Written premium per policy remains materially higher than prior to the market hardening of 2020-2022.

The reduction in U.S. Cyber written premium was predominantly driven by the top 5 writers. Written premium for the top 5 writers decreased year-over-year by 6 percent, whereas writers outside of the top 5 were more stable with a decrease in written premium of 1 percent.

The incurred loss + defense cost (DCC) ratio increased from 42 percent in 2023 to 49 percent in 2024. Despite loss ratio deterioration, there remains 51 points of margin for other expenses to maintain a combined ratio below 100 percent. Additionally, the 2024 incurred loss + DCC ratio is still at levels lower than seen during the spike in 2020 and 2021.

The performance of Primary business aligns closely with the overall industry since Primary policies account for 66 percent of earned premium in 2024. Aon Commercial Risks rate change data suggests that first Excess layer rate reductions were greater than rate reductions for Primary business, which may contribute to the higher loss ratio for Excess business. Similarly, Aon client data confirms that U.S. Micro loss ratios have outperformed other Cyber segments; much of these Micro portfolios are comprised of Endorsement business.
Exhibit 2: U.S. Cyber loss ratios | Primary / Excess / Endorsement
Increased frequency and decreased earned premium per policy outpaced reductions in severity, which led to loss ratio deterioration in 2024.

Aon Commercial Risks and reinsurance data confirm that many insurers received heightened precautionary loss notifications in 2024 due to the CrowdStrike and Change Healthcare events, many of which ultimately had negligible incurred loss. Furthermore, Aon analysis of Risk Based Security data shows rising ransomware frequency throughout most of 2024. Per Aon Global 2025 Cyber Risk Report, there is evidence that ransomware payouts declined in 2024. These observations align with the increased frequency and reduced severity seen in the NAIC Cyber supplement.

On the premium side, the impact of market softening observed in 2023 continued to earn its way into 2024 premium, contributing to a reduction in earned premium per policy and an increase in the loss ratio.
Exhibit 3: Components of loss ratio change, 2023 to 2024

In 2024, the paid-to-incurred ratio increased for the first time since 2020. Prior to this year, the rise in incurred losses relative to paid was evidence that Cyber reserves have been increasing and the tail of Cyber could be lengthening. Although 2024 does not align with the historical pattern, external factors may explain the surge in payments, such as widespread Cyber event activity and paying down reserves built up in past years.

This report utilizes individual company loss ratios for all years since the inception of the NAIC Cyber supplement to provide insight into the volatility of the U.S. Cyber market. The inclusion of 2024 in the all-year (2015-2024) coefficient-of-variation (CV) estimate - defined as standard deviation divided by mean ??? produces a CV of 136 percent, lower than the 142 percent calculated in the prior year report. For writers with greater than $5 million of written premium, the 2024 CV of 66 percent is similar to the 67 percent for 2023 and notably lower than CVs in older years. Therefore, the trend of a less volatile Cyber market continued in 2024.
A total of 218 U.S. insurers reported direct Cyber written premium to the NAIC in 2024, consistent with the count in 2023.

U.S. Cyber premiums reported to the NAIC decreased to $7.08 billion in 2024, a 2 percent decrease from the prior year. Most U.S. Cyber premium (65 percent) is from Primary business, while most policies (55 percent) are from Endorsement business. 1
Exhibit 5: U.S. Cyber direct written premiums | 2020 ??? 2024 2

To understand the factors that contributed to the lack of premium growth, policy count and written premium per policy (WP/Policy) are examined below. In 2024, policy count decreased by 0.5 percent while WP/Policy decreased by 1.8 percent. Together, the reduced policy count and premium per policy led to a 2.3 percent decrease in written premium from 2023 to 2024. The decline in written premium per policy is consistent with a Cyber market that has been softening in recent years. However, the decrease in WP/Policy from 2023 to 2024 (1.8 percent) is smaller than the decrease from 2022 to 2023 (10.2 percent).
Exhibit 6: U.S. Cyber policy count and written premium per policy (WP/Policy) | 2020 ??? 2024

2 Calendar year 2023 data was updated from what was shown in last year???s report to include an additional $63 million of written premium that was reported following publication. This has minimal impact on the findings from last year???s report, however, reiterates the importance of reviewing the data extraction date in the ???About the Data??? section and noting that this information is subject to change throughout the year.

A deeper dive into changes in WP/Policy shows a more nuanced picture. The following chart focuses on companies with at least $5 million of written premium in 2024 3. From the data, the distribution of changes to WP/Policy at an individual company level shows a wide range of outcomes with 28 percent of companies experiencing changes in the range of -10 percent to +10 percent year-over-year. The median change is a 1.5 percent increase.
Exhibit 7: Distribution of year-over year change in written premium per policy (WP/Policy) | insurers with WP greater than $5 million

In the exhibit below, both the mean WP/Policy and median change in WP/Policy are plotted over the last three years. The largest decrease in both mean and median change in WP/Policy is from 2022 to 2023. In 2024, both the mean and median change in WP/Policy are notably lower. With the caveat that rate is just one of many factors that impact premium per policy, these observations are directionally consistent with Aon???s internal data that suggests that, while there was still evidence of softening in 2024, it eased compared to 2023.
3 This premium threshold is used throughout the report to moderate the impact of outliers.

The year-over-year change in policy count differs from recent years. In 2024, the U.S. Cyber market experienced a decrease in policy count following a few years of significant growth. For reference, policy count grew 11.7 percent in 2023 and decreased 0.5 percent in 2024. However, 60 percent of writers with greater than $5 million of written premium increased policy count in 2024. While most companies continue to find opportunities to write more policies, there is a trend of policy count decreases that reflects an adherence to stricter underwriting guidelines or coverage terms and a willingness to non renew policies that do not meet updated standards. Note that this data only includes U.S. domiciled policy counts and would not reflect any changes in alien domiciled insurer policy counts.
Alien writers contribute a meaningful part of U.S. Cyber premium

The data presented throughout this report reflects the performance of U.S. Cyber business for U.S. domiciled insurers, which is the data contained in the statutory supplement. <content>The FBI???s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) released its 2025 Annual Report and the figures are sobering. matches.content: 2024 was a year of market-size stability and sub-50 percent loss ratio performance for the U.S Cyber market. U.S. Cyber written premium reported to the NAIC decreased 2 percent year-over-year to $7.1 billion in 2024. At the same time, the U.S. industry loss ratio reported to the NAIC increased by 7 points to 49 percent in 2024, driven by increased frequency and decreased earned premium per policy.

In 2024, the market felt the effects of these headwinds which may have contributed to the loss ratio deterioration outlined in this report. Widespread events such as CrowdStrike, Change Healthcare and CDK struck the market, highlighting the potential materiality of catastrophe events and the importance of reinsurance. Furthermore, ransomware frequency continues to rise amongst a softening rate environment. Despite these challenges, the U.S. industry loss ratio allows for 51 points of margin for other expenses to remain profitable, demonstrating the resilience of the U.S. Cyber market.

The incurred loss + defense cost (DCC) ratio increased from 42 percent in 2023 to 49 percent in 2024. Despite loss ratio deterioration, there remains 51 points of margin for other expenses to maintain a combined ratio below 100 percent. Additionally, the 2024 incurred loss + DCC ratio is still at levels lower than seen during the spike in 2020 and 2021.

The performance of Primary business aligns closely with the overall industry since Primary policies account for 66 percent of earned premium in 2024. Aon Commercial Risks rate change data suggests that first Excess layer rate reductions were greater than rate reductions for Primary business, which may contribute to the higher loss ratio for Excess business. Similarly, Aon client data confirms that U.S. Micro loss ratios have outperformed other Cyber segments; much of these Micro portfolios are comprised of Endorsement business.
Exhibit 2: U.S. Cyber loss ratios | Primary / Excess / Endorsement
Increased frequency and decreased earned premium per policy outpaced reductions in severity, which led to loss ratio deterioration in 2024.

Aon Commercial Risks and reinsurance data confirm that many insurers received heightened precautionary loss notifications in 2024 due to the CrowdStrike and Change Healthcare events, many of which ultimately had negligible incurred loss. Furthermore, Aon analysis of Risk Based Security data shows rising ransomware frequency throughout most of 2024. Per Aon Global 2025 Cyber Risk Report, there is evidence that ransomware payouts declined in 2024. These observations align with the increased frequency and reduced severity seen in the NAIC Cyber supplement.

On the premium side, the impact of market softening observed in 2023 continued to earn its way into 2024 premium, contributing to a reduction in earned premium per policy and an increase in the loss ratio.
Exhibit 3: Components of loss ratio change, 2023 to 2024

In 2024, the paid-to-incurred ratio increased for the first time since 2020. Prior to this year, the rise in incurred losses relative to paid was evidence that Cyber reserves have been increasing and the tail of Cyber could be lengthening. Although 2024 does not align with the historical pattern, external factors may explain the surge in payments, such as widespread Cyber event activity and paying down reserves built up in past years.

Nevertheless, third party claims continued to rise as a proportion of total reported claims, increasing from 23 percent in 2023 to 25 percent in 2024. Because third party claims tend to take more time to develop, this may put pressure on Cyber reporting and payment patterns.

This report utilizes individual company loss ratios for all years since the inception of the NAIC Cyber supplement to provide insight into the volatility of the U.S. Cyber market. The inclusion of 2024 in the all-year (2015-2024) coefficient-of-variation (CV) estimate - defined as standard deviation divided by mean ??? produces a CV of 136 percent, lower than the 142 percent calculated in the prior year report. For writers with greater than $5 million of written premium, the 2024 CV of 66 percent is similar to the 67 percent for 2023 and notably lower than CVs in older years. Therefore, the trend of a less volatile Cyber market continued in 2024.
Cyber loss ratio remains below 50 percent despite deterioration in 2024

Total direct incurred industry loss + defense cost ratio (LR) was 49 percent across all policies, an increase from the 42 percent 5 LR calculated for calendar year 2023. This is on a calendar year basis, which includes premium written in 2023 and 2024, paid losses in 2024, and reserve changes in 2024 from losses that occurred in 2024 and all prior accident years.
Exhibit 14: U.S. Cyber loss ratios | Primary / Excess / Endorsement

Although the loss ratio has deteriorated year-over-year, the 2024 loss ratio of 49 percent provides 51 points of margin for other expenses to remain a profitable line of business. At this point in time, Cyber is not a separate line on the annual statement, and therefore expense information is not available to calculate a true industry combined ratio.
Below is a longer-term view of loss ratios. Although the loss ratio increased in 2024, it remains at levels lower than experienced during the loss ratio spike of 2020 and 2021.
To better understand what the industry experienced in 2024, the table below shows a distribution of loss ratio changes for companies with at least $5 million of written premium in 2024.
Exhibit 16: Distribution of year-over year change in loss ratio | insurers with WP greater than $5 million

Although the overall loss ratio increased year-over-year, the distribution among individual insurers shows that performance change was more evenly spread between improvement and deterioration. The median change in loss ratio among insurers with WP > $5 million was 0 percent, compared to +1 percent in the prior year. Focusing on the median change provides more insight at the individual company level since larger insurer performance can drive the industry loss ratio.

However, larger writers experienced more deterioration than the market as a whole. For insurers with greater than $50 million of written premium, the median change was a 7 percent increase. Because larger insurers have more impact on the industry loss ratio, the overall industry loss ratio increased 7 points.
Spread of loss ratios increased in 2024 for writers with greater than $50 million of written premium

The chart below shows the percentile distribution of loss ratios for insurers with written premium greater than $50 million, referred to as a ???Box and Whisker??? plot. As part of the ???Box and Whisker??? plot, the 25 th, 50 th (Median) and 75 th percentile loss ratios are displayed as lines that create the ???box???, and the 1 st and 99 th percentile are shown at the tip of each whisker above and below the ???box???. In addition to percentiles, a dot within each chart represents the mean loss ratio.

Since 2021, the box plot has become more compact, suggesting that volatility of performance between insurers has reduced compared to prior years. However, in 2024, the loss ratio distribution shifted upward, as higher LRs were observed across all percentiles. In contrast to 2022 and 2023, there are more extreme outliers at the high end.
Exhibit 17: Cyber insurance loss ratio percentiles by year | insurers with WP greater than $50 million

The U.S. Cyber loss ratio increased year-over-year by 7 points. To better understand the drivers of loss ratio change, earned premium per policy, frequency and severity trends are evaluated. When considering trends, it is important to emphasize that these are insured claims only, do not reflect all Cyber incidents, and can be affected by changes in policy terms and underwriting.

In the exhibits below, it is important to note potential data quality issues that may skew overall averages. In 2023, some companies reported Cyber premium but did not report claims or incurred loss values. Consequently, the sample size of companies influencing metrics for earned premium per policy, frequency, and severity may vary.

Despite evidence of stability in the rate environment, premium earning in 2024 is a function of premium written both in 2023 and 2024. Due to the higher level of rate softening in 2023, earned premium decreased by 10 percent from $7.4 billion in 2023 to $6.6 billion in 2024. Furthermore, 54 percent of writers with at least $5 million in written premium observed a decrease in earned premium per policy, with a median change of -5 percent. At the mean, earned premium per policy decreased by 13 percent.
Overall, the loss ratios in 2024 are still feeling the effects of the softening rate environment from 2023;
Exhibit 18: U.S. Cyber earned premium per policy | 2020 ??? 2024

The increase in frequency stems from stalled policy count growth in 2024 paired with a 40 percent increase in claim count from 2023 to 2024. There are multiple factors that may cause this trend in frequency, such as increased sophistication of ransomware, AI-powered attacks, evolving threat actor tactics, and widespread events that happened throughout 2024.

Cyber catastrophe events may be suppressing severity in 2024. Anecdotally, these widespread events resulted in an influx of claims notifications, many of which have either not materialized as loss or settled within retentions. This could lead to more claims without a corresponding loss. Indeed, there was an increase in the proportion of observed claims that closed without payment in 2024.
Exhibit 21: Total claims closed without payment as a percent of total claims closed | 2020 ??? 2024
The walk from the 2023 to 2024 loss ratio is shown below. Note that median changes reflect insurers with greater than $5 million of written premium to suppress noise in the data.
Exhibit 22: Components of loss ratio change, 2023 to 2024
Surge of paid loss as a proportion of incurred loss in 2024

Historically, Cyber has been viewed as a short-tailed line of business, meaning losses tend to be reported and paid quickly. This is supported by the majority of historical claims being related to first party coverage. However, the growth of third party claim counts paired with general industry observations indicate that the tail of Cyber loss development may be lengthening in recent years. Paid to-incurred loss ratios are included in the study to understand the evolving development length of Cyber losses.

From 2020 to 2023, paid loss had decreased as a percent of incurred loss which aligns with the idea that the tail of Cyber is lengthening. However, the paid-to-incurred ratio in 2024 increased for the first time since 2020, back to levels seen in 2020. The paid-to-incurred ratio in 2023 was 55 percent, whereas the paid-to-incurred ratio in 2024 was 76 percent.

Primary and Endorsement segments have the highest paid-to-incurred ratios which are 86 percent and 83 percent, respectively. Excess policies have the lowest paid-to-incurred ratio since these are typically more complex policies with higher attachment points.

To better understand the change in paid-to-incurred ratios, calendar year incurred losses are deconstructed below between paid losses and change in reserves. Paid losses increased significantly in 2024, from $1.66 billion in 2023 to $2.45 billion. While reserves continued to increase in 2024, the rate of increase dropped. Reserve increases had been accelerating for the past few years relative to the losses that were being paid out, coinciding with the evolving nature of ransomware and business interruption losses, as well as new threat actor techniques that create third party liabilities for insurers. However, after two years of reserve increases over $1 billion in 2022 and 2023, reserve increases dipped to $792 million in 2024.

There are a few potential reasons for these changes. For one, the increase in paid loss could reflect growth in cyber expertise across the industry which may make the claims settlement process more efficient. Additionally, Cyber catastrophe events in 2024 contribute to the increase in paid loss. Lastly, after building up their reserve balances for the past few years, insurers may be paying off these older claims.
Third party claims continue to increase as a percent of total claims
In 2024, claims against third party coverage accounted for 25 percent of all claims, still meaningfully lower than first party claim counts.

However, the proportion of third party claims increased year-over-year from 23 percent in 2023 to 25 percent in 2024. Prior to 2022, third party claims had been dropping as a proportion of total, which aligns with the timing of the surge in ransomware activity during 2019 and 2020. Since then, ransomware claims have evolved and may have third party components in addition to other factors such as new threat actor techniques that may generate third party claims.

Despite the surge in payments and slowdown in reserve increases in 2024, the continued increase in third party claims is worth monitoring. This, combined with the U.S. litigation environment and the well understood development pattern of E&O claims, indicate that Cyber could be less short-tailed than generally assumed.

6 As mentioned in last year???s report, there was one company that reported a significant amount of third party Standalone claims in 2022 (45 percent of total Standalone third party claims in 2022), but now reports most of their claims as first party. If this company were removed from the data, the observed shift in first vs. third party claims would show a smooth increase in the proportion of third party claims since 2022.

As seen in the ???Cyber Loss Ratios and Profitability??? section, individual insurers saw loss ratio results both higher and lower than the industry average of 49 percent ??? some notably so. Among writers with at least $5 million of direct written premium, loss ratios ranged from 2 percent at the low end to 124 percent at the high end.

The coefficient of variation (CV) of insurer loss ratios ??? standard deviation divided by the mean ??? is shown below. For insurers with at least $5 million of direct written premium (WP), the All-Year CV has decreased year-over-year with the inclusion of 2024 data. This is consistent with the 2024 CV being a point lower than the 2023 CV, and the CVs for both years being materially reduced from what had been observed in older years. For insurers with at least $50 million of direct written premium (WP), the all year CV has decreased 2 points year-over-year.
Exhibit 26: Coefficient of variation of direct loss ratio by year

To dive deeper into the CV calculations above, the standard deviation in 2024 increased compared to 2023, which is consistent with the wider spread of loss ratios observed in the ???Cyber Loss Ratios and Profitability??? section. However, the mean loss ratio increased in 2024 by more than the standard deviation which led to the 2024 CV being lower than the 2023 CV.

In the additional analysis below, the CVs are normalized for differences between companies. This shines a light on how the observed volatility is driven by certain companies having consistently lower/higher Cyber loss ratios than others, versus other factors, such as volatility between years or randomness within an individual company???s results. This adjustment aims to strip out the volatility between companies from the calculated CVs.
Exhibit 28: Coefficient of variation of direct loss ratio with adjustment for volatility between companies

"WHO GLASS 2023 bloodstream isolates: Acinetobacter carbapenem resistance 54.3% globally, African E. coli 3GC 70.7%, SE Asia K. pneumoniae carbapenem 41.2%, EMR MRSA 50.3% ??? last-line and first-choice failure rates mapped by pathogen and WHO region.",
"Dark navy cinematic bloodstream corridor with crimson bacterial nodes and cyan WHO regional resistance arcs",

content: `Bloodstream infections are the severity end of bacterial disease ??? and the place where antibiotic failure shows up first in global surveillance. WHO???s Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) now publishes adjusted 2023 estimates across more than **23 million** bacteriologically confirmed infections from **104** reporting countries. This desk cut asks one question: **which pathogen???drug cells, and which WHO regions, post the highest share of bloodstream isolates resistant to last-line and first-choice drugs?**

The interactive dashboard above is built as a **resistant-isolate share lens**. Toggle **Peak cells**, **Regions**, **Trends**, and **US vs GLASS**. On peaks, filter last-line carbapenems versus first-choice agents. On regions, flip among Acinetobacter carbapenem, *K. pneumoniae* carbapenem, *E. coli* carbapenem, *K. pneumoniae* 3GC, *E. coli* 3GC, and MRSA. The punchline is multi-cell, not a single slogan. Globally, **Acinetobacter ?? imipenem** sits at **54.3%** resistant (95% CrI 49.3???59.2). African Region *E. coli* third-generation cephalosporin resistance hits **70.7%**. South-East Asia *K. pneumoniae* carbapenem resistance reaches **41.2%**. Eastern Mediterranean MRSA bloodstream share is **50.3%**. Same surveillance system ??? four different failure tips.
| *K. pneumoniae* ?? cefotaxime | African Region | **77.8%** | First-choice Watch 3GC |
| Acinetobacter ?? imipenem | African Region | **71.0%** | Last-line carbapenem |
| *E. coli* ?? 3GC | African Region | **70.7%** | SDG AMR indicator pair |
| *E. coli* ?? cefotaxime | South-East Asia | **67.3%** | First-choice tip |
| Acinetobacter ?? imipenem | Eastern Mediterranean | **66.5%** | Last-line regional peak |
| *S. aureus* ?? methicillin | Eastern Mediterranean | **50.3%** | MRSA BSI |
| *K. pneumoniae* ?? imipenem | South-East Asia | **41.2%** | Last-line Klebsiella tip |
| *E. coli* ?? imipenem | South-East Asia | **17.5%** | Low level, steep slope |

Read the table as a **family of peak cells**, not one global average. Carbapenem rows are the last-line story: Acinetobacter already fails more than half the time globally, and regional peaks push into the high sixties and seventies. Third-generation cephalosporin rows are the first-choice story: *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae* lose the drugs clinicians reach for first, especially in Africa and South-East Asia. MRSA is a separate Gram-positive lane ??? lower globally at **27.1%**, but still one in two bloodstream isolates in the Eastern Mediterranean Region.

Despite loss ratio deterioration, there remains 51 points of margin for other expenses to maintain a combined ratio below 100 percent. For the first time since 2020, the overall proportion of written premium from domestic insurers has decreased from 75 percent in 2022 to 74 percent in 2023. Domestic Package premium decreased as a proportion of total Package premium from 86 percent in 2022 to 77 percent in 2023; for Standalone business, these proportions were more consistent at 71 percent in 2022 and 72 percent in 2023.
Below is a longer-term view of loss ratios. Although the loss ratio increased in 2024, it remains at levels lower than experienced during the loss ratio spike of 2020 and 2021.

Since 2021, the box plot has become more compact, suggesting that volatility of performance between insurers has reduced compared to prior years. However, in 2024, the loss ratio distribution shifted upward, as higher LRs were observed across all percentiles. In contrast to 2022 and 2023, there are more extreme outliers at the high end.

From 2020 to 2023, paid loss had decreased as a percent of incurred loss which aligns with the idea that the tail of Cyber is lengthening. However, the paid-to-incurred ratio in 2024 increased for the first time since 2020, back to levels seen in 2020. The paid-to-incurred ratio in 2023 was 55 percent, whereas the paid-to-incurred ratio in 2024 was 76 percent.

Synthesis:
Ransomware is consistently identified as the most costly and disruptive type of cyber claim, even as its share of total claim volume remains lower than business email compromise or funds transfer fraud [1][2][3]. For Coalition policyholders in 2025, ransomware claims severity averaged $292,000, reflecting a 7% decrease from 2024 levels alongside a 3% dip in claim frequency [1][2]. While ransom demands surged 47% in 2025 to over $1 million, 86% of victims refused to pay, and incident response teams continued to negotiate significant reductions for those who did [4].

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

/**

export const CONTENT = `US cyber insurance looked like a growth story that finally paid for itself. Direct written premium at U.S.-domiciled insurers climbed from about **$2.75 billion** in 2020 to roughly **$7.26 billion** in 2022, then stalled near **$7.25 billion** in 2023. Over the same hard-market climb, calendar-year loss ratios compressed from an estimated mid-to-high-sixties spike into the mid-forties. The desk question for 2026 is narrower and sharper: **did written premium grow faster than incurred losses ??? and, inside those losses, how concentrated is the severity tip in ransomware?**

The interactive dashboard above is built as a **premium-versus-loss race**, not a marketing pitch for capacity. Toggle **Premium vs loss race**, **Loss ratio + growth**, **Ransomware concentration**, and **Paid / structure**. On the race panel, flip domestic NAIC prints against the broader market that adds alien surplus lines. On ransomware, switch claim-volume mix, constructed severity-dollar mix, and the FBI IC3 complaint-loss ladder so the insurance map and the crime-complaint map refuse to be averaged into one slogan.

## The scoreboard: premium stalled, loss ratio rebounded

| Metric | 2023 | 2024 | Read |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Domestic DWP | **$7.25B** | **$7.08B** | First clear soft print after the hard market |
| Total DWP (incl. alien surplus) | **$9.84B** | **$9.14B** | ???7.1% ??? broader market also shrank |
| Calendar loss ratio (loss + DCC) | **42%** | **49%** | +7 points of pressure |
| Earned premium | **$7.4B** | **$6.6B** | Soft rates earning through |
| Paid losses | **$1.66B** | **$2.45B** | Paid-to-incurred 55% ??? 76% |
| Approx. incurred (earned ?? LR / paid+reserve) | **~$3.11B** | **~$3.24B** | Incurred still rising as premium falls |
| Claims reported (order of magnitude) | ??? | **~50,000** | ~+40% frequency |

Read the table as a **two-clock story**. Clock one is premium: the 2020???2022 compounding that made cyber a capacity magnet has stopped, and 2024 is the first NAIC year where both the domestic and total-market prints fall. Clock two is loss: frequency jumped, earned premium per policy fell, and the industry loss ratio gave back seven points even though it remains sub-50% ??? still leaving roughly **51 points** of expense margin before a 100 combined ratio on this calendar print.

## Did premium grow faster than incurred losses?

Yes ??? **through the hardening years**. Domestic written premium rose about **+75%** in 2021 and another **+50%** in 2022. Reconstructed incurred dollars rose too, but far more slowly once rates and underwriting standards caught up: roughly **+61%** then only about **+7%** as the 2022 loss ratio printed near **45%**. Indexed to 2020 = 100, premium ran well ahead of incurred through 2022???2023. That is the arithmetic behind the ???cyber finally works??? narrative that flooded broker decks.

**2023 and 2024 reverse the race.** Premium growth went flat (???0.2%) then negative (???2.3% domestic; ???7.1% including alien surplus). Incurred kept grinding higher on a reconstructed path even as the 2023 loss ratio dipped to **42%**. In 2024, earned premium fell about **10%** to **$6.6B** while the loss ratio jumped to **49%**, so approximate incurred settled near **$3.24B** ??? a modest absolute increase that still **narrows the premium???loss gap** because the premium base is shrinking at the same time claims frequency is rising.

The punchline is not that cyber suddenly became unprofitable on a calendar loss+DCC basis. It is that **the premium outrun is over**. Hard-market years bought margin by growing the denominator faster than the numerator. Soft-market years shrink the denominator while frequency and catastrophe notifications push the numerator. That is a different risk-transfer regime than the 2021???2022 story.

## Loss ratio mechanics: frequency up, severity mixed, rates soft

Aon???s extraction of the NAIC Cybersecurity & Identity Theft Supplement attributes the 2024 deterioration to a familiar insurance triangle: **more claims**, **less earned premium per policy**, and **severity that did not fall enough to offset**. Claim counts rose on the order of **40%**, with nearly **50,000** reports. Written premium per policy slipped about **1.8%**, and earned premium ??? which still carries soft 2023 pricing ??? dropped harder.

Severity is messier. Broking and claims desks saw ransomware **frequency** re-accelerate while **average ransom payments** and negotiated severities cooled in parts of the book. At the same time, 2024 delivered several **systemic notifications** ??? CrowdStrike, Change Healthcare, CDK ??? that flooded precautionary claim files, many of which closed with little or no payment. That mix can inflate **frequency** and the share of claims closed without payment while still lifting paid dollars as older reserves convert to cash.

Paid losses jumped from **$1.66B** to **$2.45B**. Reserve increases slowed to about **$792M** after two years of billion-dollar-plus builds. The paid-to-incurred ratio therefore snapped from **55%** to **76%**. That is not proof the line has shortened forever; third-party claim share still crept from **23%** to **25%**, and third-party cyber liability develops more like professional liability than a same-quarter ransom invoice.

## How concentrated are losses in ransomware?

Concentration depends on **which ledger** you open.

On an **insured claims book** (Coalition???s 2024 policyholder experience, used here as a transparent public cut ??? not a NAIC census), **business email compromise and funds-transfer fraud** dominate **claim count** at about **60%**. Ransomware is closer to **one-fifth** of events ??? about **21%** ??? but sits at the **severity tip**, with average ransomware severity on that book in the high-two-hundreds of thousands of dollars. A simple volume??severity index on that mix puts ransomware near **two-fifths** of constructed severity dollars even though it is not the volume majority. That is concentration of **loss dollars**, not concentration of **incident tickets**.

On the **FBI IC3 2024 complaint ledger**, the picture flips. Total reported internet-crime losses hit about **$16.6 billion**. Investment fraud alone cleared roughly **$6.6B**; BEC about **$2.8B**. Ransomware complaints numbered **3,156**, with reported ransomware losses near **$12.5 million** ??? a rounding error against the fraud stack, and a known **undercount** relative to business interruption, forensics, and remediation that never hit an IC3 form. Ransomware remains the most pervasive threat to critical-infrastructure complainants; it is **not** where IC3 dollars concentrate.

Do not average those two maps. Insurance severity cares about **business interruption, extortion, restoration, and liability** attached to insured events. IC3 dollars care about **what victims report to a crime desk**, which skews toward fraud and consumer loss. Ransomware can be the insurance market???s severity engine while looking tiny on a crime-complaint pie.

## Policy structure still concentrates the premium base

Primary policies still take about **65%** of 2024 domestic written premium, excess about **31%**, and endorsements about **4%**. Endorsements flip the volume story: they are a large share of **policies in force** but a thin share of **dollars**, which is why average premium-per-policy statistics move when the endorsement mix shifts. Excess layers absorbed more rate softening in broker data, which helps explain why excess loss ratios can run hotter than primary even when the industry average stays under 50%.

Writer concentration matters too. The top five domestic writers drove most of the 2024 premium decline (???6% among the tip versus about ???1% outside it). When the tip softens first, industry DWP can fall even while mid-tier writers still add policies. That is a capacity-pricing story as much as a demand story.

## Caveats and measurement traps

Several traps will invent fake conclusions if you ignore them.

**Domestic versus total market.** NAIC statutory supplement prints cover U.S.-domiciled writers (**$7.08B** DWP in 2024). The NAIC Cybersecurity Insurance Report???s broader perimeter that includes alien surplus lines is larger (**$9.14B**) and fell harder (???7.1%). Mixing the two without a label invents a growth rate that exists in neither series.

**Calendar-year loss ratios are not accident-year ultimates.** The 49% print includes reserve changes on prior years. A soft-rate year can look worse on calendar LR even if the accident-year cohort eventually develops differently ??? and the reverse is also true.

**Incurred dollars for earlier years are reconstructed.** 2023???2024 earned premium, paid loss, and reserve change are disclosed in the Aon NAIC extraction. Earlier incurred points in the dashboard are constructed from earned proxies and estimated spike-era loss ratios; treat them as **directional**, not as a substitute for a full Schedule P.

**Carrier claim-mix is not a census.** Coalition???s BEC/ransomware shares illuminate severity concentration on one active book. Other carriers??? micro, mid-market, and large-account mixes will differ. The dashboard tags constructed severity-dollar shares accordingly.

**IC3 ??? insurance.** Equating **$12.5M** of IC3 ransomware losses with NAIC incurred cyber losses is a category error. Use IC3 for crime-complaint composition and critical-infrastructure threat ranking; use NAIC for the risk-transfer ledger.

**Catastrophe notifications are not catastrophe paid losses.** 2024???s widespread events raised claim counts and desk load; many files closed without payment. Frequency spikes can precede severity spikes ??? or evaporate.

## What the 2026 desk should watch next

Three meters decide whether the premium???loss race stays closed.

First, **earned premium per policy** as soft 2023???2024 rates finish earning. If written rates stabilize while earned keeps falling, calendar loss ratios can rise without a new frequency shock.

Second, **ransomware severity versus frequency**. Frequency can rise while average ransom paid falls ??? good for victims, ambiguous for insurers if business-interruption days stretch and dual-extortion liability thickens.

Third, **third-party claim share and paid-to-incurred**. A sustained climb in third-party mix plus another surge in paid cash is the early warning that cyber???s ???short-tail??? folklore is aging out.

Until those meters turn, the honest 2026 print is this: **US cyber written premium did grow faster than incurred losses through the hard market; that outrun ended as 2024 premium fell and the loss ratio jumped to 49%. Ransomware still concentrates insured severity even when it is a minority of claim tickets and a rounding error on the IC3 dollar ladder.**`;

Clock two is loss: frequency jumped, earned premium per policy fell, and the industry loss ratio gave back seven points even though it remains sub-50% ??? still leaving roughly **51 points** of expense margin before a 100 combined ratio on this calendar print.

## Did premium grow faster than incurred losses?

Yes ??? **through the hardening years**. Domestic written premium rose about **+75%** in 2021 and another **+50%** in 2022. Reconstructed incurred dollars rose too, but far more slowly once rates and underwriting standards caught up: roughly **+61%** then only about **+7%** as the 2022 loss ratio printed near **45%**. Indexed to 2020 = 100, premium ran well ahead of incurred through 2022???2023. That is the arithmetic behind the ???cyber finally works??? narrative that flooded broker decks.

**2023 and 2024 reverse the race.** Premium growth went flat (???0.2%) then negative (???2.3% domestic; ???7.1% including alien surplus). Incurred kept grinding higher on a reconstructed path even as the 2023 loss ratio dipped to **42%**. In 2024, earned premium fell about **10%** to **$6.6B** while the loss ratio jumped to **49%**, so approximate incurred settled near **$3.24B** ??? a modest absolute increase that still **narrows the premium???loss gap** because the premium base is shrinking at the same time claims frequency is rising.

The punchline is not that cyber suddenly became unprofitable on a calendar loss+DCC basis. It is that **the premium outrun is over**. Hard-market years bought margin by growing the denominator faster than the numerator. Soft-market years shrink the denominator while frequency and catastrophe notifications push the numerator. That is a different risk-transfer regime than the 2021???2022 story.

## Loss ratio mechanics: frequency up, severity mixed, rates soft

Aon???s extraction of the NAIC Cybersecurity & Identity Theft Supplement attributes the 2024 deterioration to a familiar insurance triangle: **more claims**, **less earned premium per policy**, and **severity that did not fall enough to offset**. Claim counts rose on the order of **40%**, with nearly **50,000** reports. Written premium per policy slipped about **1.8%**, and earned premium ??? which still carries soft 2023 pricing ??? dropped harder.

Severity is messier. Broking and claims desks saw ransomware **frequency** re-accelerate while **average ransom payments** and negotiated severities cooled in parts of the book. At the same time, 2024 delivered several **systemic notifications** ??? CrowdStrike, Change Healthcare, CDK ??? that flooded precautionary claim files, many of which closed with little or no payment. That mix can inflate **frequency** and the share of claims closed without payment while still lifting paid dollars as older reserves convert to cash.

Paid losses jumped from **$1.66B** to **$2.45B**. Reserve increases slowed to about **$792M** after two years of billion-dollar-plus builds. The paid-to-incurred ratio therefore snapped from **55%** to **76%**. That is not proof the line has shortened forever; third-party claim share still crept from **23%** to **25%**, and third-party cyber liability develops more like professional liability than a same-quarter ransom invoice.

## How concentrated are losses in ransomware?

Concentration depends on **which ledger** you open.

On an **insured claims book** (Coalition???s 2024 policyholder experience, used here as a transparent public cut ??? not a NAIC census), **business email compromise and funds-transfer fraud** dominate **claim count** at about **60%**. Ransomware is closer to **one-fifth** of events ??? about **21%** ??? but sits at the **severity tip**, with average ransomware severity on that book in the high-two-hundreds of thousands of dollars. A simple volume??severity index on that mix puts ransomware near **two-fifths** of constructed severity dollars even though it is not the volume majority. That is concentration of **loss dollars**, not concentration of **incident tickets**.

On the **FBI IC3 2024 complaint ledger**, the picture flips. Total reported internet-crime losses hit about **$16.6 billion**. Investment fraud alone cleared roughly **$6.6B**; BEC about **$2.8B**. Ransomware complaints numbered **3,156**, with reported ransomware losses near **$12.5 million** ??? a rounding error against the fraud stack, and a known **undercount** relative to business interruption, forensics, and remediation that never hit an IC3 form. Ransomware remains the most pervasive threat to critical-infrastructure complainants; it is **not** where IC3 dollars concentrate.

Do not average those two maps. Insurance severity cares about **business interruption, extortion, restoration, and liability** attached to insured events. IC3 dollars care about **what victims report to a crime desk**, which skews toward fraud and consumer loss. Ransomware can be the insurance market???s severity engine while looking tiny on a crime-complaint pie.

## Policy structure still concentrates the premium base

Primary policies still take about **65%** of 2024 domestic written premium, excess about **31%**, and endorsements about **4%**. Endorsements flip the volume story: they are a large share of **policies in force** but a thin share of **dollars**, which is why average premium-per-policy statistics move when the endorsement mix shifts. Excess layers absorbed more rate softening in broker data, which helps explain why excess loss ratios can run hotter than primary even when the industry average stays under 50%.

Writer concentration matters too. The top five domestic writers drove most of the 2024 premium decline (???6% among the tip versus about ???1% outside it). When the tip softens first, industry DWP can fall even while mid-tier writers still add policies. That is a capacity-pricing story as much as a demand story.

## Caveats and measurement traps

Several traps will invent fake conclusions if you ignore them.

**Domestic versus total market.** NAIC statutory supplement prints cover U.S.-domiciled writers (**$7.08B** DWP in 2024). The NAIC Cybersecurity Insurance Report???s broader perimeter that includes alien surplus lines is larger (**$9.14B**) and fell harder (???7.1%). Mixing the two without a label invents a growth rate that exists in neither series.

**Calendar-year loss ratios are not accident-year ultimates.** The 49% print includes reserve changes on prior years. A soft-rate year can look worse on calendar LR even if the accident-year cohort eventually develops differently ??? and the reverse is also true.

**Incurred dollars for earlier years are reconstructed.** 2023???2024 earned premium, paid loss, and reserve change are disclosed in the Aon NAIC extraction. Earlier incurred points in the dashboard are constructed from earned proxies and estimated spike-era loss ratios; treat them as **directional**, not as a substitute for a full Schedule P.

**Carrier claim-mix is not a census.** Coalition???s BEC/ransomware shares illuminate severity concentration on one active book. Other carriers??? micro, mid-market, and large-account mixes will differ. The dashboard tags constructed severity-dollar shares accordingly.

**IC3 ??? insurance.** Equating **$12.5M** of IC3 ransomware losses with NAIC incurred cyber losses is a category error. Use IC3 for crime-complaint composition and critical-infrastructure threat ranking; use NAIC for the risk-transfer ledger.

**Catastrophe notifications are not catastrophe paid losses.** 2024???s widespread events raised claim counts and desk load; many files closed without payment. Frequency spikes can precede severity spikes ??? or evaporate.

## What the 2026 desk should watch next

Three meters decide whether the premium???loss race stays closed.

First, **earned premium per policy** as soft 2023???2024 rates finish earning. If written rates stabilize while earned keeps falling, calendar loss ratios can rise without a new frequency shock.

Second, **ransomware severity versus frequency**. Frequency can rise while average ransom paid falls ??? good for victims, ambiguous for insurers if business-interruption days stretch and dual-extortion liability thickens.

Third, **third-party claim share and paid-to-incurred**. A sustained climb in third-party mix plus another surge in paid cash is the early warning that cyber???s ???short-tail??? folklore is aging out.

Until those meters turn, the honest 2026 print is this: **US cyber written premium did grow faster than incurred losses through the hard market; that outrun ended as 2024 premium fell and the loss ratio jumped to 49%. Ransomware still concentrates insured severity even when it is a minority of claim tickets and a rounding error on the IC3 dollar ladder.**`;
